title: The Founding of CERN
text:
After the Second World War, European physics was in ruins. Many of its best scientists had fled to the United States, and no single European country could afford the giant accelerators that modern nuclear physics required. A handful of scientists, among them the French physicist Louis de Broglie, Isidor Rabi of the United States, and Pierre Auger and Edoardo Amaldi in Europe, began arguing for a shared laboratory.

At a UNESCO conference in Florence in 1950, Rabi formally proposed that European countries pool their resources. Over the next three years diplomats and physicists hammered out the details. In 1952 a provisional council was created, whose French initials, CERN, became the name. A site was chosen at Meyrin, near Geneva in Switzerland.

The convention establishing the organization was signed in 1953 by twelve countries, among them nations that had been at war less than a decade before, including France, the United Kingdom and West Germany. It came into force on 29 September 1954, after enough governments had ratified it. The convention stated that the laboratory would have no concern with military work and that its results would be published or otherwise made generally available.

CERN's first accelerator started up in 1957. The laboratory grew into one of the world's leading centers of physics, with scientists from many nations working side by side. In 1989 a CERN researcher, Tim Berners-Lee, proposed the system that became the World Wide Web.
lesson: Former enemies can build something together when a shared goal is too big for any of them alone. Openness about results helps keep trust between partners.
people: Isidor Rabi, Louis de Broglie, Pierre Auger, Edoardo Amaldi
source: Convention for the Establishment of a European Organization for Nuclear Research (1953); Armin Hermann et al., History of CERN, vol. 1 (1987)
